Austrian physicist (1887–1961), born and died in Vienna, and one of the founders of quantum mechanics.
In 1926 he published the wave equation that bears his name, which describes how a quantum system's wave function changes over time. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac.
His 1944 book What Is Life? asked how physics could explain heredity and influenced the early molecular biologists.
A thought experiment Person/Erwin Schrödinger published in 1935 to show how strange the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics becomes when a Superposition reaches an everyday object.

Schrödinger worked the idea out in letters with Person/Albert Einstein after the 1935 EPR paper. Einstein had proposed a keg of gunpowder that is both exploded and unexploded; Schrödinger replaced it with a cat.
It appears in "Die gegenwärtige Situation in der Quantenmechanik" ("The Present Situation in Quantum Mechanics"), Naturwissenschaften, 1935.
A sealed box holds a cat, a flask of hydrocyanic acid, a small radioactive sample and a Geiger counter wired to a hammer.
If an atom decays within the hour, the counter trips the hammer, the flask breaks and the cat dies. If none decays, the cat lives.

Quantum mechanics describes the atom as a superposition of decayed and undecayed. Carried through the apparatus, the whole box, cat included, ends up in a superposition of dead and alive until someone opens it.
Copenhagen — opening the box is a measurement that collapses the superposition into one outcome.
Many-worlds — both outcomes happen, in branches of reality that no longer interact.
Decoherence — interaction with the environment resolves the superposition into classical outcomes long before anyone looks, which is why large objects never show superposition.
Schrödinger meant the cat as a reductio ad absurdum. He called the dead-and-alive cat an absurdity of the existing view, and never offered it as a picture of how the world works.
French economist at MIT, where she is Abdul Latif Jameel Professor of Poverty Alleviation and Development Economics.

Co-founder and co-director of J-PAL, and winner of the 2019 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Abhijit Banerjee and Michael Kremer for the experimental approach to alleviating global poverty.
Known for breaking large social problems into testable questions and using field experiments to evaluate what actually improves outcomes.

Her posture toward AI reads as pragmatic rather than skeptical: she is interested in using machine learning where it helps target programs better, while keeping the focus on measurable human outcomes.
A recurring theme in her work is distributed capability building through education, not just centralized expertise.
She has invested heavily in open and blended teaching formats so people outside MIT can learn the tools of policy evaluation and apply them locally.
Through MITx and the DEDP MicroMasters, she helped build a model for teaching policy evaluation at global scale.
That work emphasizes that people should be able to learn rigorous methods wherever they are, then reuse them in their own institutions and contexts.
The same orientation shows up in her broader research program: train more people, share methods widely, and let knowledge travel instead of remaining concentrated in a few elite centers.
In public remarks, she has described machine learning as useful for understanding where programs are most effective and where limited budgets should be deployed.
That fits her larger style: AI as an applied tool inside evaluation and decision-making, not as a substitute for policy judgment or ground-truth evidence.
